contents.html: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in Federal information systems.

contents.html: This report, which was drafted by the National Security Council (NSC) Cyber Interagency Policy Committee’s International Cybersecurity Standardization Working Group for the Administration, sets out proposed United States Government (USG) strategic objectives for pursuing the development and use of international standards for cybersecurity, and makes recommendations to achieve those objectives. Implementation of these recommendations—which cover interagency coordination, collaboration with the U.S. private sector and international partners, agency participation in international standards development, standards training and education, use of international standards to achieve mission and policy objectives, and other topics–will enable the development and execution of a wide-ranging United States Government cybersecurity standardization strategy.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書は、政権のために、国家安全保障会議（NSC）のサイバー省庁間政策委員会の国際サイバーセキュリティ標準化作業部会が起草したもので、サイバーセキュリティに関する国際標準の策定と利用を追求するための米国政府（USG）の戦略目標の案を示し、それらの目標を達成するための勧告を行っています。これらの勧告は、省庁間の調整、米国の民間部門および国際的なパートナーとの連携、各機関による国際標準開発への参加、標準に関する訓練と教育、任務および政策目標を達成するための国際標準の利用、その他の話題を対象としており、その実施によって、広範にわたる米国政府のサイバーセキュリティ標準化戦略を策定し、実行できるようになります。

contents.html: The Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014 was signed into law by President Obama on December 18, 2014. Section 502 of the Act requires the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to work with relevant federal agencies to ensure interagency coordination “in the development of international technical standards related to information system security,” and develop and transmit to Congress a plan for ensuring such coordination within one year of enactment. Further, the Act instructs NIST to ensure consultation with “appropriate private sector stakeholders.” This report will also serve as the basis of the required report to Congress.
contents.html_ja: 2014 年サイバーセキュリティ強化法（Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014）は、2014 年 12 月 18 日にオバマ大統領が署名して成立しました。同法の第 502 条は、国立標準技術研究所（NIST）の所長に対し、関係する連邦機関と協力して、「情報システムのセキュリティに関する国際技術標準の策定」における省庁間の調整を確保すること、およびそのような調整を確保するための計画を、制定から 1 年以内に策定して議会に送付することを求めています。さらに同法は、NIST に対し、「適切な民間部門の利害関係者」との協議を確保するよう指示しています。本報告書は、求められている議会向けの報告書の基礎としても用いられます。

contents.html: Resilience is the ability of both the private sector and the government “to reduce the magnitude and/or duration of disruptive events [to critical infrastructure]. contents.html: The U.S. standardization community is comprised largely of non-governmental Standards Developing Organizations (SDOs). These groups are primarily shaped by industry (both U.S. and foreign), academic institutions, professional societies, consumer groups, and nonprofits and are motivated by market forces, public interest, and consumer protection. USG participation is motivated by the need to achieve economic, timely and effective solutions for mission and policy objectives. These diverse motivations are mutually beneficial.
contents.html_ja: 米国の標準化コミュニティは、主に非政府の標準開発組織（SDO）で構成されています。これらの団体は、主に産業界（米国および外国の双方）、学術機関、専門家団体、消費者団体、非営利団体によって形作られており、市場の力、公共の利益、消費者保護を動機としています。米国政府の参加は、任務および政策目標に対して、経済的で、適時かつ効果的な解決策を実現する必要性を動機としています。これらの多様な動機は、相互に利益をもたらします。

contents.html: For purposes of this report, a standard is a document, established by consensus and approved by a recognized body, which provides for common and repeated use, rules, guidelines or characteristics for activities or their results, aimed at the achievement of the optimum degree of order in a given context.<sup>6</sup> A standards developer is any organization that develops and approves standards using various methods to establish consensus among its participants. The use of such documentary consensus standards is voluntary.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書では、標準とは、コンセンサスによって確立され、認知された団体によって承認された文書であり、特定の状況における最適な秩序の達成を目的として、活動またはその結果に関する規則、ガイドライン、または特性を、共通かつ繰り返し使用できる形で提供するものを指します。<sup>6</sup>標準策定者とは、参加者間のコンセンサスを確立するためのさまざまな方法を用いて、標準を策定し承認する組織を指します。このような文書化されたコンセンサス標準の利用は、自主的なものです。

contents.html: Pursuant to U.S. laws and policy,<sup>7</sup> federal agencies are required to use voluntary consensus standards in their procurement and regulatory activities, giving preference to international standards, except where inconsistent with law or otherwise impractical. Many SDOs operate through a process that is characterized by all or some of the following attributes: openness, balance, due process, ability to appeal, and consensus. Openness means that the procedures or processes used are open to interested parties. Such parties are provided meaningful opportunities to participate in standards development on a non-discriminatory basis. The procedures or processes for participating in standards development and for developing the standard are transparent. The standards development process should also be balanced. Specifically, there should be meaningful involvement from a broad range of parties, with no single interest dominating the decision-making. Due process should include documented and publicly available policies and procedures, adequate notice of meetings and standards development, sufficient time to review drafts and prepare views and objections, access to views and objections of other participants and a fair and impartial process for resolving conflicting views. An appeals process should be available for the impartial handling of procedural appeals. Consensus is defined as general agreement, but not necessarily unanimity. During the development of consensus, comments and objections are considered using fair, impartial, open, and transparent processes. These process attributes contribute to the technical soundness and market relevance of the published standards of an SDO.
contents.html_ja: 米国の法律および政策<sup>7</sup>に従い、連邦機関は、調達活動および規制活動において自主的なコンセンサス標準を使用することが求められており、法律に反する場合やその他の理由で実際的でない場合を除き、国際標準を優先します。多くの SDO は、開放性、均衡、適正手続、不服申立ての可能性、コンセンサスのすべてまたは一部によって特徴付けられるプロセスを通じて運営されています。開放性とは、用いられる手続またはプロセスが関心を持つ当事者に開かれていることを意味します。そのような当事者には、差別なく標準開発に参加する実質的な機会が与えられます。標準開発への参加と標準の策定のための手続またはプロセスは、透明です。標準開発プロセスは、均衡のとれたものであるべきです。具体的には、幅広い当事者が実質的に関与し、単一の利害関係者が意思決定を支配することがないようにすべきです。適正手続には、文書化され公開されている方針と手順、会議および標準開発についての十分な通知、草案を確認し見解や異議を準備するための十分な時間、他の参加者の見解や異議を閲覧できること、相反する見解を解決するための公正で公平なプロセスが含まれるべきです。手続上の不服申立てを公平に扱うため、不服申立てのプロセスが利用できるべきです。コンセンサスとは、全員一致である必要はないものの、全般的な合意と定義されます。コンセンサスの形成中は、公正、公平、オープン、かつ透明なプロセスを用いて、意見と異議が検討されます。これらのプロセスの特性は、SDO が公表する標準の技術的な健全性と市場との関連性に寄与します。

contents.html: The U.S. standards system differs significantly from the government-driven, centrally-coordinated standards systems common in many other countries. Within the United States, there are hundreds of SDOs, which are overwhelmingly private sector organizations, providing the infrastructure for the preparation of standards documents. USG personnel participate in SDO activities along with representatives from industry, academia, and other organizations and consumers. In many other countries' standards systems, the government plays a larger role in standards development-related activities, which provides those governments the ability to use standards to support domestic industrial and innovation policy, rather than to advance technical solutions in support of public policy goals. While Federal agencies possess certain responsibilities related to standards, such as in their own use of standards or in their development of technical regulations, there is a much greater reliance in the U.S. on the private sector, including companies and industry groups, academic institutions, professional societies, consumer groups, and other interested parties, in standards development. The United States Standards Strategy<sup>8</sup>, elaborated through a private and public sector partnership in 2000, and revised most recently in 2010, outlines the contribution of private-sector led standards development to overall competition and innovation in the U.S. economy and the imperative of public and private sector participation that is a central tenet of the U.S. approach to standardization.
contents.html_ja: 米国の標準システムは、他の多くの国で一般的な、政府主導で中央集権的に調整される標準システムとは大きく異なります。米国内には数百の SDO があり、その圧倒的多数は民間部門の組織で、標準文書の作成のための基盤を提供しています。米国政府の職員は、産業界、学術機関、その他の組織や消費者の代表者とともに、SDO の活動に参加しています。他の多くの国の標準システムでは、政府が標準開発に関連する活動でより大きな役割を果たしており、そのため、それらの政府は、公共政策の目標を支える技術的解決策を推進するのではなく、標準を用いて国内の産業政策やイノベーション政策を支えることができます。連邦機関は、自らによる標準の利用や技術規則の策定など、標準に関する一定の責務を負っていますが、米国では、標準開発において、企業や業界団体、学術機関、専門家団体、消費者団体、その他の関心を持つ当事者を含む民間部門への依存がはるかに大きくなっています。2000 年に官民のパートナーシップによって作成され、直近では 2010 年に改訂された米国標準戦略（United States Standards Strategy）<sup>8</sup>は、民間部門主導の標準開発が米国経済全体の競争とイノベーションにもたらす貢献と、米国の標準化の取り組みの中心的な原則である官民双方の参加の必要性を概説しています。

contents.html: Conformity assessment is activity that provides demonstration that specified requirements relating to a product, process, system, person or body are fulfilled. Conformity assessment activities can be performed by many types of organizations or individuals. Conformity assessment can be conducted by: (1) a first party, which is generally the supplier or manufacturer; (2) a second party, which is generally the purchaser or user of the product; (3) a third party, which is an independent entity that is generally distinct from the first or second party and has no interest in transactions between the two parties; and (4) the government, which has a unique role in conformity assessment activities related to regulatory requirements.
contents.html_ja: 適合性評価とは、製品、プロセス、システム、人、または団体に関する規定された要件が満たされていることを実証する活動です。適合性評価の活動は、さまざまな種類の組織または個人が実施できます。適合性評価を実施できるのは、(1) 一般に供給者または製造者である第一者、(2) 一般に製品の購入者または利用者である第二者、(3) 一般に第一者または第二者とは別個の独立した主体で、両者間の取引に利害関係を持たない第三者、(4) 規制要件に関連する適合性評価の活動において固有の役割を持つ政府です。

contents.html: For example, conformance testing captures the technical description of the requirements in a standard and measures whether an implementation (product, process or service) faithfully fulfills these requirements. Conformance testing alone does not completely ensure the interoperability or performance of conforming products, processes, or services. Therefore, interoperability and performance testing are also important aspects for procurements. Interoperability testing tests one implementation with another to establish that they can work together properly. Performance testing measures the performance characteristics of an implementation, such as its throughput<sup>9</sup> or response time,<sup>10</sup> under various conditions.
contents.html_ja: たとえば、適合性テストは、標準に含まれる要件の技術的な記述を把握し、実装（製品、プロセス、またはサービス）がこれらの要件を忠実に満たしているかどうかを測定します。適合性テストだけでは、適合する製品、プロセス、またはサービスの相互運用性や性能を完全に保証することはできません。そのため、相互運用性テストと性能テストも、調達にとって重要な側面です。相互運用性テストは、ある実装を別の実装と組み合わせてテストし、それらが適切に連携できることを確認します。性能テストは、さまざまな条件下での、スループット<sup>9</sup>や応答時間<sup>10</sup>など、実装の性能特性を測定します。

contents.html: The World Trade Organization (WTO) Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT Agreement) – which has been implemented in U.S. law by the Trade Agreements Act of 1979, as amended (TAA)<sup>11</sup> – highlights the important role that international standards can play in facilitating trade and requires the use of relevant international standards, where effective and appropriate, in a Member’s technical regulations. Although the TBT Agreement does not identify specific international standardizing bodies, the WTO Committee on Technical Barriers to Trade has identified several principles that functionally define international standards (i.e., standards developed in processes characterized by transparency, openness, impartiality and consensus, relevance and effectiveness, coherence and accounting for developing country interests).<sup>12</sup>
contents.html_ja: 世界貿易機関（WTO）の貿易の技術的障害に関する協定（TBT 協定）は、米国では Trade Agreements Act of 1979, as amended (TAA)<sup>11</sup> によって国内法に実施されており、貿易の円滑化において国際標準が果たしうる重要な役割を強調するとともに、加盟国の技術規則において、有効かつ適切な場合には、関連する国際標準を使用することを求めています。TBT 協定は特定の国際標準化団体を指定していませんが、WTO の貿易の技術的障害に関する委員会は、国際標準を機能面から定義するいくつかの原則（すなわち、透明性、開放性、公平性とコンセンサス、関連性と有効性、一貫性、開発途上国の利益への配慮を特徴とするプロセスで策定された標準）を特定しています。<sup>12</sup>

contents.html: The International Strategy for Cyberspace<sup>13</sup> lays out an approach to unify USG engagement with international partners on a full range of cyber issues. The International Strategy highlights the need to develop and use international cybersecurity standards and conformity assessment schemes, and the importance of public-private sector collaboration. The Strategy establishes the goal that “[t]he United States will work internationally to promote an open, interoperable, secure, and reliable information and communications infrastructure that supports international trade and commerce, strengthens international security, and fosters free expression and innovation.” The strategy contains policy priorities for the economy; protecting our networks; law enforcement; military; internet governance; international development; and internet freedom. This includes steps to enhance confidence in cyberspace and pursue those who would exploit online systems, and a commitment from the USG to participate actively in discussions about how international norms and measures on cybercrime are developed bilaterally and multilaterally, in fora with proven expertise and a history of promoting effective cybercrime policies. This also includes promoting processes to permit states to investigate, apprehend, and prosecute those who intrude or disrupt networks.
contents.html_ja: サイバー空間に関する国際戦略（International Strategy for Cyberspace）<sup>13</sup>は、サイバーに関するあらゆる問題について、国際的なパートナーと米国政府の関与を統一するための取り組み方を示しています。この国際戦略は、サイバーセキュリティの国際標準と適合性評価スキームを策定し利用する必要性と、官民の連携の重要性を強調しています。同戦略は、「米国は、国際貿易と商取引を支え、国際安全保障を強化し、表現の自由とイノベーションを育む、開かれた、相互運用可能で、安全かつ信頼できる情報通信インフラストラクチャを促進するために、国際的に取り組む」という目標を掲げています。この戦略には、経済、ネットワークの保護、法執行、軍事、インターネットガバナンス、国際開発、インターネットの自由についての政策上の優先事項が含まれています。これには、サイバー空間における信頼を高め、オンラインシステムを悪用する者を追及するための措置や、効果的なサイバー犯罪対策を推進してきた実績と専門知識を持つフォーラムにおいて、サイバー犯罪に関する国際的な規範と措置が二国間および多国間でどのように策定されるかという議論に積極的に参加するという、米国政府の公約が含まれます。また、国家がネットワークへの侵入や妨害を行う者を調査し、逮捕し、訴追できるようにするプロセスの促進も含まれます。

contents.html: The National Cooperative Research Act of 1984<sup>14</sup> first allowed organizations to collaborate to carry out joint research and development ventures and not be deemed illegal per se under federal antitrust laws or similar State laws. One result has been a rapid growth in IT consortia developing standards. In developing their standards, many of these consortia follow the WTO TBT Committee Decision principles. However, consortia are also formed that are not open, with membership by invitation. Consortia range from unincorporated affiliations of companies to incorporated entities with budgets, offices and paid staff. A consortium may exist to complete a specific standard, but others have a broader mission and develop multiple standards necessary to enable the evolution of a category of business services and products. An oft-cited advantage of IT consortia is speed in developing a standard, but speed is sometimes obtained due to a greater alignment in the technical interests of the participating entities. However, the narrow alignment of the interests of the participating entities may not represent a broad need, and this may slow uptake of the developed standard. At the same time, rapid innovation in emerging technologies has been accompanied by competition among SDOs to undertake new work areas in emerging fields of standardization that are perceived to be of great market relevance (e.g., smart grid, cloud computing, cybersecurity). This competitive environment has encouraged most SDOs to streamline their consensus building processes in order to develop and approve technically sound standards that meet current market needs in an effective manner.
contents.html_ja: 1984 年の National Cooperative Research Act<sup>14</sup>は、組織が共同で研究開発事業を実施することを初めて認め、連邦の反トラスト法や類似の州法のもとでそれ自体が違法とはみなされないようにしました。その結果の 1 つとして、標準を策定する IT コンソーシアムが急速に増加しました。これらのコンソーシアムの多くは、標準の策定にあたり、WTO TBT 委員会決定の原則に従っています。しかし、オープンではなく、加盟が招待制であるコンソーシアムも設立されています。コンソーシアムは、法人格のない企業の連合から、予算、事務所、有給の職員を持つ法人組織まで、さまざまです。特定の標準を完成させるために存在するコンソーシアムもあれば、ビジネスサービスや製品の特定のカテゴリの発展を可能にするために必要な複数の標準を策定する、より広範な使命を持つものもあります。IT コンソーシアムの利点としてしばしば挙げられるのは、標準の策定の速さですが、その速さは、参加する主体の技術的な関心がより一致していることによって得られる場合もあります。ただし、参加する主体の関心が狭い範囲で一致しているだけでは、幅広いニーズを表していない可能性があり、それが策定された標準の採用を遅らせることがあります。同時に、新興技術における急速なイノベーションに伴い、市場との関連性が非常に大きいと見られる標準化の新興分野（例: スマートグリッド、クラウドコンピューティング、サイバーセキュリティ）での新たな作業分野を担うための、SDO 間の競争が生じています。この競争的な環境により、ほとんどの SDO は、現在の市場のニーズを満たす技術的に健全な標準を効果的に策定し承認するために、コンセンサス形成のプロセスを合理化するようになりました。

contents.html: Memorandum M-12-08<sup>15</sup> on “Principles for Federal Engagement in Standards Activities to Address National Priorities” provides guidance to agencies with respect to their engagement in standards activities that have been identified as national priorities either through executive branch or Congressional actions. For example, “Agencies considering a convening or active engagement role in private sector standards developing organizations in order to address a national priority area should state their reasons plainly (including why private sector leadership alone is insufficient). Further, agencies should accept and act on feedback on their rationales before assuming this convening or active-engagement role in a private sector standards developing organization. In all cases, agencies should ensure effective intra- and inter-agency coordination of engagement in standards development activities. When an agency commits to a cooperative standards development effort with industry, that commitment should be maintained, as resources permit, and the resulting standards should be used where feasible. Agencies should use existing processes and, where necessary, establish new processes for open, transparent, and effective two-way communication with private sector interests, ensuring that concerns from private sector entities are given thorough and objective consideration. To the extent feasible and appropriate, agencies should also provide continuous support for their technical experts' participation and leadership activities in mission-critical standards-setting activities and standards organizations, including standards organization-specific training and mentoring. Agencies should periodically review their standards activities to identify gaps in representation for mission-critical areas as part of their long-range planning and adopt policies that value and reward participation in standardization activities.”
contents.html_ja: 覚書 M-12-08<sup>15</sup>「国家的優先事項に対処するための標準化活動への連邦の関与に関する原則（Principles for Federal Engagement in Standards Activities to Address National Priorities）」は、行政府または議会の措置を通じて国家的優先事項として特定された標準化活動への関与について、各機関に指針を示しています。たとえば、「国家的優先分野に対処するために、民間部門の標準開発組織で招集役または積極的な関与の役割を担うことを検討している機関は、その理由（民間部門のリーダーシップだけでは不十分である理由を含む）を明確に述べるべきです。さらに、機関は、民間部門の標準開発組織でこの招集役または積極的な関与の役割を担う前に、その根拠に対するフィードバックを受け入れ、それに基づいて行動すべきです。あらゆる場合において、機関は、標準開発活動への関与に関する、機関内および機関間の効果的な調整を確保すべきです。機関が産業界との協調的な標準開発の取り組みに参加を約束した場合、その約束は、資源が許す限り維持されるべきであり、その結果として策定された標準は、実行可能な場合には使用されるべきです。機関は、既存のプロセスを用い、必要な場合には新たなプロセスを確立して、民間部門の関係者との間で、オープンで透明性があり効果的な双方向のコミュニケーションを確保し、民間部門の主体からの懸念が徹底的かつ客観的に検討されるようにすべきです。実行可能かつ適切な範囲で、機関は、任務上不可欠な標準設定活動および標準化組織における技術専門家の参加とリーダーシップ活動に対して、標準化組織固有のトレーニングやメンタリングを含め、継続的な支援を提供すべきです。機関は、長期計画の一環として、自らの標準化活動を定期的に見直し、任務上不可欠な分野における代表者の不足を特定するとともに、標準化活動への参加を評価し報いる方針を採用すべきです。」

contents.html: This section sets out core areas of cybersecurity that broadly influence the overall cybersecurity of products, processes, services, and organizations. USG technical experts have been participating in many core areas of cybersecurity standardization for decades. The resulting standards are largely being developed for the global marketplace generally and not just for federal networks and applications.<sup>16</sup> Such standards provide the requirements for cybersecurity standards-based products, processes or services. As a consequence of participating in this standards work, the USG has acquired and accumulated competency in core areas of cybersecurity standardization, but the depth and breadth of this USG competency can rise and fall with time.
contents.html_ja: 本節では、製品、プロセス、サービス、組織の全体的なサイバーセキュリティに広く影響を与える、サイバーセキュリティの中核分野を示します。米国政府の技術専門家は、サイバーセキュリティ標準化の多くの中核分野に、数十年にわたって参加してきました。その結果として策定される標準は、連邦のネットワークやアプリケーションだけのためではなく、主にグローバル市場全般を対象としています。<sup>16</sup>こうした標準は、サイバーセキュリティ標準に基づく製品、プロセス、サービスの要件を提供します。この標準化作業に参加した結果、米国政府はサイバーセキュリティ標準化の中核分野における能力を獲得し蓄積してきましたが、この米国政府の能力の深さと広さは、時間とともに増減することがあります。

contents.html: Core areas of cybersecurity standardization include: cryptographic techniques; cyber incident management; identity and access management; IT system security evaluation; information security management systems; network security; security automation and continuous monitoring; supply chain risk management; software assurance; and system security engineering. These areas, which are relevant for numerous applications, are discussed in detail in the Supplemental Information document (NISTIR 8074 Volume 2). Based upon legislative and policy mandates, there are a growing number of national priority applications for which the USG participates in the development of standards relevant to cybersecurity, including: cloud computing; emergency management; industrial control systems; health IT; smart grid; and voting. Such applications utilize cybersecurity standards in each of the listed core areas.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティ標準化の中核分野には、暗号技術、サイバーインシデント管理、ID およびアクセス管理、IT システムのセキュリティ評価、情報セキュリティマネジメントシステム、ネットワークセキュリティ、セキュリティ自動化および継続的監視、サプライチェーンのリスク管理、ソフトウェア保証、システムセキュリティエンジニアリングが含まれます。これらの分野は多数のアプリケーションに関連しており、補足情報の文書（NISTIR 8074 Volume 2）で詳しく論じています。法令および政策上の義務付けに基づき、米国政府がサイバーセキュリティに関連する標準の策定に参加している国家的優先アプリケーションは増えつつあり、クラウドコンピューティング、緊急事態管理、産業用制御システム、医療 IT、スマートグリッド、投票があります。こうしたアプリケーションは、挙げられた各中核分野のサイバーセキュリティ標準を利用しています。

contents.html: <sup>16</sup> That said, the national and economic security of the United States depends on the reliable functioning of critical infrastructure, which is largely owned and operated by the private sector. Recognizing this, the President issued Executive Order 13636, Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, in February 2013 (http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/FR-2013-02-19/pdf/2013-03915.pdf). It directed NIST to work with stakeholders to develop a voluntary framework – based on existing standards, guidelines, and practices — for reducing cyber risks to critical infrastructure. NIST released the first version of the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (http://www.nist.gov/cyberframework/upload/cybersecurity-framework-021214-final.pdf) on February 12, 2014. The Framework, created through collaboration between industry and government, consists of standards, guidelines, and practices to promote the protection of critical infrastructure by helping owners and operators of critical infrastructure to manage cyber security related risk.
contents.html_ja: <sup>16</sup> とはいえ、米国の国家安全保障と経済安全保障は、主に民間部門が所有し運用する重要インフラストラクチャの確実な機能に依存しています。これを認識して、大統領は 2013 年 2 月に大統領令 13636「重要インフラストラクチャのサイバーセキュリティの向上（Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity）」（http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/FR-2013-02-19/pdf/2013-03915.pdf）を発出しました。この大統領令は、NIST に対し、利害関係者と協力して、既存の標準、ガイドライン、実践に基づき、重要インフラストラクチャに対するサイバーリスクを低減するための自主的なフレームワークを策定するよう指示しました。NIST は、2014 年 2 月 12 日に、Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity（http://www.nist.gov/cyberframework/upload/cybersecurity-framework-021214-final.pdf）の初版を公表しました。このフレームワークは、産業界と政府の協力によって作成され、重要インフラストラクチャの所有者と運用者がサイバーセキュリティに関連するリスクを管理するのを支援することで、重要インフラストラクチャの保護を促進するための標準、ガイドライン、実践で構成されています。

contents.html: Worldwide, there are over 200 SDOs developing IT and ICS standards. Among those, there are dozens of SDOs developing cybersecurity standards, yet fewer SDOs may develop international cybersecurity standards. Some of the key SDOs directly involved in cybersecurity that may develop international standards are: the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP); the 3rd Generation Partnership Project 2 (3GPP2); the Alliance for Telecommunications Industry Solutions (ATIS); the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA); the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI); the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC); the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE); the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); the International Society of Automation (ISA); the International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission Joint Technical Committee 1 (ISO/IEC JTC 1), Information Technology; the International Organization for Standardization Technical Committee 68 (ISO TC 68), Financial Services; the International Telecommunication Union Radiocommunication Sector (ITU-R); the Object Management Group (OMG); the OpenID Foundation (OIDF); the Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards (OASIS); the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council (PCI SSC); SAE International; The Open Group; the Trusted Computing Group (TCG); the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C); and the WiMAX Forum. Collectively, these SDOs have many hundreds of cybersecurity standards projects under maintenance or development. Being able to influence cybersecurity standards development requires developing and maintaining effective liaisons and active engagements within and among these SDOs.

contents.html: Four observations can be made on the overall status of ongoing cybersecurity standardization. First, robust standardization activities in the listed core areas of cybersecurity standardization are undoubtedly necessary for ensuring interoperability, security, usability, and resilience. Second, as illustrated by the listed applications in Table 1, there is a mix of ongoing standardization and maintenance of existing standards that is necessary to sustain deployments of standards-based products, processes and services. Third, the standards produced by SDOs represent a point in time. They often need to evolve in a way that meets the challenges of the ever-changing threat landscape. Finally, while Table 1 is structured by applications, there are some cybersecurity standards that apply across the applications to the development and manufacturing of IT products (hardware and software), products that most if not all of these applications depend on.

contents.html: There are at least three active USG groups that provide for interagency coordination on standards-related matters. The Interagency Committee on Standards Policy (ICSP) provides advice and recommendations to the Secretary of Commerce and other Executive Branch agencies on matters related to standards policy that could impact Federal agencies’ participation in, and use of, standards. The Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) Subcommittee of the Trade Policy Staff Committee (TPSC), which is led by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), coordinates the development and implementation of USG positions relating to technical regulations, standards and conformity assessment procedures around the world. The JESC (Joint Enterprise Standards Committee) serves as the Department of Defense (DoD) information technology standards and Intelligence Community (IC) enterprise standards governance body. This forum collaborates and recommends common enterprise standards, profiles, and specifications for the respective DoD and IC information environments. Interagency coordination on standards-related matters also occurs in some subcommittees and working groups within the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC). Given the critical importance of cybersecurity standardization and its cross-cutting nature —which involves security, standards, innovation, competition, trade, privacy, law enforcement and national security, and other policy considerations –a higher-level interagency coordination mechanism is needed. Coordination by senior Federal cybersecurity officials under the auspices of the Executive Office of the President (EOP) would provide the necessary focus and resources to develop and implement a strategy for cybersecurity-related standardization, as well as ensure that the USG can respond to specific priority issues as they arise.
contents.html_ja: 標準に関する事項について省庁間の調整を行う、活動中の米国政府のグループが少なくとも 3 つあります。標準政策省庁間委員会（Interagency Committee on Standards Policy: ICSP）は、連邦機関による標準への参加と標準の利用に影響しうる標準政策に関する事項について、商務長官およびその他の行政府機関に助言と勧告を行います。通商代表部（USTR）が主導する通商政策スタッフ委員会（TPSC）の貿易の技術的障害（TBT）小委員会は、世界各地の技術規則、標準、適合性評価手続に関する米国政府の立場の策定と実施を調整します。JESC（Joint Enterprise Standards Committee）は、国防総省（DoD）の情報技術標準およびインテリジェンスコミュニティ（IC）のエンタープライズ標準のガバナンス組織として機能します。このフォーラムは、DoD と IC それぞれの情報環境に共通するエンタープライズ標準、プロファイル、仕様について協力し、勧告します。標準に関する事項についての省庁間の調整は、国家科学技術会議（NSTC）内の一部の小委員会および作業部会でも行われています。サイバーセキュリティ標準化が極めて重要であること、およびセキュリティ、標準、イノベーション、競争、貿易、プライバシー、法執行と国家安全保障、その他の政策上の考慮事項にまたがる分野横断的な性質を持つことから、より上位の省庁間調整の仕組みが必要です。大統領府（EOP）の主導のもとで、連邦政府のサイバーセキュリティ担当の上級職員が調整を行えば、サイバーセキュリティ関連の標準化戦略を策定し実施するために必要な焦点と資源が得られるとともに、米国政府が、特定の優先課題が生じたときに対応できるようにすることができます。

contents.html: In addition to coordination among federal agencies, the USG needs to engage effectively with U.S. industry. There are several methods agencies use to engage and coordinate with external stakeholders. Agencies may choose to establish external advisory committees per the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), seek input using Federal Register Notice solicitations, use specific statutory or regulatory authority to create a forum — such as a private sector coordinating council — for obtaining input, establish a public-private partnership, or use some other method that provides all potential stakeholders an equal opportunity to provide input and share their perspectives. As an example of FACA committees, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) created Health IT Policy and Standards committees that make recommendations to the National Coordinator on policy and standards topics, including cybersecurity. In addition, in developing the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity under Executive Order 13636, NIST provided stakeholders with an equal opportunity to share their views and make contributions through a series of workshops and public comment periods on drafts.
contents.html_ja: 連邦機関間の調整に加えて、米国政府は米国産業界と効果的に関与する必要があります。機関が外部の利害関係者と関与し調整するために用いる方法は、いくつかあります。機関は、連邦諮問委員会法（FACA）に従って外部の諮問委員会を設置すること、連邦官報の通知による募集を用いて意見を求めること、民間部門調整評議会のようなフォーラムを設けて意見を得るために特定の法律上または規則上の権限を用いること、官民パートナーシップを設けること、またはすべての潜在的な利害関係者に意見の提供と見解の共有の平等な機会を与えるその他の方法を用いることを選択できます。FACA 委員会の例として、米国保健福祉省（HHS）は、サイバーセキュリティを含む政策および標準の話題について全国調整官（National Coordinator）に勧告を行う、医療 IT の政策委員会と標準委員会を設置しました。また、NIST は、大統領令 13636 に基づく Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity の策定にあたり、一連のワークショップと草案に対するパブリックコメント期間を通じて、利害関係者が見解を共有し貢献する平等な機会を提供しました。

contents.html: For SDOs that use a national body member process, such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), there is already built-in U.S. coordination through U.S. mirror groups (e.g., U.S. Technical Advisory Groups (TAGs) for ISO technical committees and subcommittees). For SDOs that are based on an individual membership model, public-private sector coordination prior to technical committee meetings is not built-in, so this may be a particular area that could benefit from enhanced focus by the USG.

contents.html: The protection of individual privacy promotes U.S. interests by facilitating improved trust in online and offline transactions and helping U.S. products and services compete in global markets. Cybersecurity is an important component of protecting privacy, and many privacy standards address the protection of personal data by cross-referencing standards in the area of information security management systems. Nonetheless, cybersecurity measures also can create privacy risks. Executive Order (E.O.) 13636<sup>17</sup> recognized this concern by requiring the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to include a methodology to protect privacy and civil liberties in the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity.<sup>18</sup> The NIST Roadmap for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity<sup>19</sup> referred to how few technical standards or best practices exist to mitigate the impact of cybersecurity activities on individual privacy and civil liberties. It is in the best interests of the USG to support the development and use of cybersecurity standards that minimize risks to privacy, promote information-sharing relating to cybersecurity, and allow the USG to combat cyber-enabled threats. Greater understanding of how to identify privacy risks and integrate mitigations into cybersecurity standards or their deployment in information systems will require further research.
contents.html_ja: 個人のプライバシーの保護は、オンラインおよびオフラインの取引に対する信頼の向上を促し、米国の製品とサービスがグローバル市場で競争する助けとなることにより、米国の利益を促進します。サイバーセキュリティはプライバシー保護の重要な構成要素であり、多くのプライバシー標準は、情報セキュリティマネジメントシステムの分野の標準を相互参照することで、個人データの保護を扱っています。しかしながら、サイバーセキュリティ対策がプライバシーリスクを生じさせることもあります。大統領令（E.O.）13636<sup>17</sup>は、NIST に対し、Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity<sup>18</sup>にプライバシーと市民的自由を保護するための方法論を含めるよう求めることで、この懸念を認識しました。NIST Roadmap for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity<sup>19</sup>は、サイバーセキュリティ活動が個人のプライバシーと市民的自由に及ぼす影響を緩和するための技術標準やベストプラクティスが、ほとんど存在しないことに言及しました。プライバシーへのリスクを最小限に抑え、サイバーセキュリティに関する情報共有を促進し、米国政府がサイバーを利用した脅威に対処できるようにするサイバーセキュリティ標準の策定と利用を支援することは、米国政府の最善の利益にかないます。プライバシーリスクを特定し、その緩和策をサイバーセキュリティ標準または情報システムへのその展開に統合する方法について、より深く理解するには、さらなる研究が必要です。

contents.html: <sup>17</sup> E.O. 13636, Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, February 12, 2013 notes: “Repeated cyber intrusions into critical infrastructure demonstrate the need for improved cybersecurity. The cyber threat to critical infrastructure continues to grow and represents one of the most serious national security challenges we must confront. The national and economic security of the United States depends on the reliable functioning of the Nation's critical infrastructure in the face of such threats. It is the policy of the United States to enhance the security and resilience of the Nation's critical infrastructure and to maintain a cyber environment that encourages efficiency, innovation, and economic prosperity while promoting safety, security, business confidentiality, privacy, and civil liberties. We can achieve these goals through a partnership with the owners and operators of critical infrastructure to improve cybersecurity information sharing and collaboratively develop and implement risk-based standards.” (Section 1) http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/FR-2013-02-19/pdf/2013-03915.pdf.
contents.html_ja: <sup>17</sup> E.O. 13636, Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, February 12, 2013 は次のように述べています。「重要インフラストラクチャに対するサイバー侵入が繰り返されていることは、サイバーセキュリティの向上が必要であることを示しています。重要インフラストラクチャに対するサイバー脅威は増大し続けており、われわれが立ち向かわなければならない最も深刻な国家安全保障上の課題の 1 つです。米国の国家安全保障と経済安全保障は、そのような脅威に直面しても、国の重要インフラストラクチャが確実に機能することに依存しています。米国の政策は、国の重要インフラストラクチャのセキュリティとレジリエンスを高め、安全、セキュリティ、事業上の機密性、プライバシー、市民的自由を促進しつつ、効率性、イノベーション、経済的繁栄を促すサイバー環境を維持することです。これらの目標は、重要インフラストラクチャの所有者および運用者とのパートナーシップを通じて、サイバーセキュリティ情報共有を改善し、リスクベースの標準を共同で策定し実施することによって達成できます。」（Section 1）http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/FR-2013-02-19/pdf/2013-03915.pdf。

contents.html: Maintaining and, where needed, augmenting USG competency in the core areas of cybersecurity standardization require continuous education, participation and training. Obtaining a consensus to approve standards among participants in various SDOs usually requires more than a simple majority but less than unanimity. Effective negotiation in standards development requires not just technical expertise by Federal agency participants, but a thorough knowledge of an SDO’s standards development process and policies, as well as soft skills in negotiating with stakeholders with a range of often diverse and conflicting positions. In addition, awareness of the relevant market and associated market politics that drive the motivations of the other participants is essential. For international fora, understanding the culture of the participants is also important. Accordingly, continuity in participation is crucial to success. Participants must regularly attend the meetings, have established relationships with the other participants, and ensure that the draft standards are technically sound and meet USG needs. Effective leadership in SDOs promotes timely development of technically sound standards.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティ標準化の中核分野における米国政府の能力を維持し、必要に応じて強化するには、継続的な教育、参加、トレーニングが必要です。さまざまな SDO の参加者間で標準を承認するコンセンサスを得るには、通常、単純過半数を超え、全会一致には満たない支持が必要です。標準開発における効果的な交渉には、連邦機関の参加者の技術的な専門知識だけでなく、SDO の標準開発プロセスと方針についての十分な知識、および、しばしば多様で相反するさまざまな立場の利害関係者と交渉するためのソフトスキルが必要です。さらに、他の参加者の動機となる関連市場と、それに伴う市場の駆け引きについて理解していることが不可欠です。国際的なフォーラムでは、参加者の文化を理解することも重要です。したがって、参加の継続性は成功に不可欠です。参加者は、会議に定期的に出席し、他の参加者との関係を築き、標準の草案が技術的に健全で、米国政府のニーズを満たすようにしなければなりません。SDO における効果的なリーダーシップは、技術的に健全な標準の時宜を得た策定を促します。

Candidates for such leadership positions should be both technically knowledgeable and thoroughly familiar with the SDO’s development processes and policies, and have a good understanding of USG and U.S. industry priorities and perspectives. This is critical for effective communication and information-sharing and ultimately will assist in advancing the USG’s strategic objectives in each SDO. The Framework can be used to identify opportunities for new or revised standards, guidelines, or practices that would help organizations address emerging needs.

contents.html: Maintaining USG competency to participate effectively in the development of new or revised core cybersecurity standards areas provides the foundation to respond to ever-evolving USG priorities. The development of international standards for cybersecurity promotes U.S. interests by facilitating interoperability, security, usability and resilience; improving trust in online and offline transactions; promoting innovation and competitiveness; and helping U.S. products and services compete in global markets. Increased and more strategic and coordinated U.S. engagement in cybersecurity standardization will help promote U.S. interests by ensuring that standards-based requirements for cybersecurity products, processes, and services meet U.S. objectives. Ensuring effective U.S. leadership in the relevant standards developing bodies for cybersecurity requires awareness of specific SDO environments, coordination of USG interests with U.S. industry and organization interests to prioritize and achieve U.S. objectives, and a robust focus on education and training.

The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in Federal information systems.

This interagency report sets out proposed United States Government (USG) strategic objectives for pursuing the development and use of international standards for cybersecurity and makes recommendations to achieve those objectives. The recommendations cover interagency coordination, collaboration with the U.S. private sector and international partners, agency participation in international standards development, standards training and education, use of international standards to achieve mission and policy objectives, and other issues. NISTIR 8074 Volume 2, Supplemental Information for the Interagency Report on Strategic U.S. Government Engagement in International Standardization to Achieve U.S. Objectives for Cybersecurity, provides additional background on international cybersecurity standardization.

 Cybersecurity is “the prevention of damage to, unauthorized use of, or exploitation of, and, if needed, the restoration of electronic information and communications systems and the information contained therein to ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability.”3

 Resilience is the ability of both the private sector and the government “to reduce the magnitude and/or duration of disruptive events [to critical infrastructure]. The effectiveness of a resilient infrastructure or enterprise depends upon its ability to anticipate, absorb, adapt to, and/or rapidly recover from a potentially disruptive event.”4

o Ensuring that there is a sufficient inventory of international standards that can serve as a basis for the cybersecurity and resilience of U.S. organizations, particularly critical infrastructure. This includes both cybersecurity standards and standards from other domains that are relevant to cybersecurity.
o Using international standards as a key part of USG procurement policy to support secure and resilient operations.

o Ensuring that international standards meet the cybersecurity interests of the USG including protecting against illicit cyber activities or actions by terrorist groups, cybercriminals, and hostile nation-state actors.

o Supporting the development and use of new standards by taking into account: the scope of standardization work of candidate SDOs, U.S. industry preferences, USG needs, and the recent track record of candidate SDOs in particular areas of cybersecurity standardization.

o Developing technically sound, reasonably available5, and fit for purpose standards in open, transparent, and consensus-based processes, and updating as often as necessary in collaboration with the private sector.

o Supporting the development and use of international standards and associated assessment schemes for cybersecurity (where relevant, effective, and appropriate), which can promote international trade and provide a level playing field for U.S. companies.
o Ensuring market relevance by developing standards in response to industry, government and consumer requirements and timelines.
o Supporting the development and use of international standards in collaboration with U.S. industry, to foster open and fair competition.
o Promoting the inclusion of existing and emerging technologies in international standards that boost U.S. competitiveness and ensuring that USG equities are well represented in those standards.

o Encouraging the development and use of performance-based standards for cybersecurity, where appropriate. Cybersecurity standards with performance-based requirements are more likely to encourage innovation and enable competition than standards based upon prescriptive design requirements. Prescriptive design standards are sometimes necessary, however, particularly for describing test methods or procedures.

 The World Trade Organization (WTO) Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT Agreement) – which has been implemented in U.S. law by the Trade Agreements Act of 1979, as amended (TAA)11 – highlights the important role that international standards can play in facilitating trade and requires the use of relevant international standards, where effective and appropriate, in a Member’s technical regulations. Although the TBT Agreement does not identify specific international standardizing bodies, the WTO Committee on Technical Barriers to Trade has identified several principles that functionally define international standards (i.e., standards developed in processes characterized by transparency, openness, impartiality and consensus, relevance and effectiveness, coherence and accounting for developing country interests).12

 The International Strategy for Cyberspace13 lays out an approach to unify USG engagement with international partners on a full range of cyber issues. The International Strategy highlights the need to develop and use international cybersecurity standards and conformity assessment schemes, and the importance of public-private sector collaboration. The Strategy establishes the goal that “[t]he United States will work internationally to promote an open, interoperable, secure, and reliable information and communications infrastructure that supports international trade and commerce, strengthens international security, and fosters free expression and innovation.” The strategy contains policy priorities for the economy; protecting our networks; law enforcement; military; internet governance; international development; and internet freedom. This includes steps to enhance confidence in cyberspace and pursue those who would exploit online systems, and a commitment from the USG to participate actively in discussions about how international norms and measures on cybercrime are developed bilaterally and multilaterally, in fora with proven expertise and a history of promoting effective cybercrime policies. This also includes promoting processes to permit states to investigate, apprehend, and prosecute those who intrude or disrupt networks.

 The National Cooperative Research Act of 198414 first allowed organizations to collaborate to carry out joint research and development ventures and not be deemed illegal per se under federal antitrust laws or similar State laws. One result has been a rapid growth in IT consortia developing standards. In developing their standards, many of these consortia follow the WTO TBT Committee Decision principles. However, consortia are also formed that are not open, with membership by invitation. Consortia range from unincorporated affiliations of companies to incorporated entities with budgets, offices and paid staff. A consortium may exist to complete a specific standard, but others have a broader mission and develop multiple standards necessary to enable the evolution of a category of business services and products. An oft-cited advantage of IT consortia is speed in developing a standard, but speed is sometimes obtained due to a greater alignment in the technical interests of the participating entities. However, the narrow alignment of the interests of the participating entities may not represent a broad need, and this may slow uptake of the developed standard. At the same time, rapid innovation in emerging technologies has been accompanied by competition among SDOs to undertake new work areas in emerging fields of standardization that are perceived to be of great market relevance (e.g., smart grid, cloud computing, cybersecurity). This competitive environment has encouraged most SDOs to streamline their consensus building processes in order to develop and approve technically sound standards that meet current market needs in an effective manner.

 Memorandum M-12-0815 on “Principles for Federal Engagement in Standards Activities to Address National Priorities” provides guidance to agencies with respect to their engagement in standards activities that have been identified as national priorities either through executive branch or Congressional actions. For example, “Agencies considering a convening or active engagement role in private sector standards developing organizations in order to address a national priority area should state their reasons plainly (including why private sector leadership alone is insufficient). Further, agencies should accept and act on feedback on their rationales before assuming this convening or active-engagement role in a private sector standards developing organization. In all cases, agencies should ensure effective intra- and inter-agency coordination of engagement in standards development activities. When an agency commits to a cooperative standards development effort with industry, that commitment should be maintained, as resources permit, and the resulting standards should be used where feasible. Agencies should use existing processes and, where necessary, establish new processes for open, transparent, and effective two-way communication with private sector interests, ensuring that concerns from private sector entities are given thorough and objective consideration. To the extent feasible and appropriate, agencies should also provide continuous support for their technical experts' participation and leadership activities in mission-critical standards-setting activities and standards organizations, including standards organization-specific training and mentoring. Agencies should periodically review their standards activities to identify gaps in representation for mission-critical areas as part of their long-range planning and adopt policies that value and reward participation in standardization activities.”
 Participating in limited specific activities is following, contributing to, and/or leading a specific standards effort for a select activity(s) specific to unique needs or interests.
 Monitoring focuses on broader programs of work and emerging and evolving standards produced by the SDOs. It includes developing an understanding of, and relationships with, the key players.

 Influencing, in addition to the requirements of monitoring, involves commenting on, and providing contributions to, strategically important standards, working with industry and international players, and exerting influence through formal and informal discussions and provision of expertise.

 Leading involves the activities associated with monitoring and influencing and, additionally, providing leadership through roles such as convening or administering consensus groups, serving as the standards project editor, and serving as the liaison representative between standards groups. Such leadership roles require that the official act in accordance with the duties assigned by the SDO and not advocate on behalf of his or her agency or country.

 The National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (NICE)20: The goal of NICE is to establish an operational, sustainable and continually improving national cybersecurity education program that will develop sound cyber practices to enhance the nation’s security. The scope of this program includes the Federal workplace, civilians, and students in kindergarten through post-graduate school.

 The NIST Standards Services Curricula Development Cooperative Agreement Program provides financial assistance to support curriculum development for the undergraduate and/or graduate level. This Program supports the integration of documentary and measurement standards and standardization information and content into seminars, courses, and learning resources.

 Many U.S. based private sector entities also run relevant standards education and curricular development activities and welcome USG participation and collaboration. These include, but are not limited to, the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), which has programs and content to raise awareness of the importance of standards and conformity assessment among university faculty in engineering, technology, business, public policy and law schools21. Similarly, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) runs a broad Standards Education program22 to promote knowledge of standards and the importance of standardization among students. Other unique standards education-related resources are available from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) at Education about standards23. The NIST Standards.gov web pages include standards training resources of agencies, SDOs, universities, etc.

 The Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity24 developed under Executive Order 13636 provides a prioritized, flexible, repeatable, performance-based, and cost-effective approach to manage cybersecurity risk for those processes, information, and systems directly involved in the delivery of critical infrastructure services. The Framework relies on standards for its use, with “Informative References” containing specific sections of standards, guidelines, and practices common among critical infrastructure sectors. The Framework can be used to identify opportunities for new or revised standards, guidelines, or practices that would help organizations address emerging needs.
 The USG should strengthen its high-level interagency coordination process for cybersecurity standardization.
o Such a mechanism should help to ensure that both internal agency and overall USG efforts are well coordinated, both within the USG and with relevant private sector stakeholders.

o Agencies participating in the work of specific SDOs would have an established interagency venue for developing objectives and strategies in concert with interagency colleagues, as well as raising, and where possible coordinating on, major issues.
 Federal agencies should regularly highlight within their agencies the need to participate in standards development for cybersecurity in pursuit of their agency’s mission and objectives.
 Federal agencies should support a long-term commitment of resources and participants with specialized knowledge, skills and abilities for international cybersecurity standardization.

 The USG should maintain and, where needed, augment its competency in core areas of cybersecurity standardization. As part of their long-range planning, Federal agencies should periodically review their standards participation to identify gaps in representation for mission-critical activities.

 Federal agencies should value and reward staff participation in standardization activities, encourage junior staff members to be involved in standardization activities, and provide mechanisms for recognition of effective participation by their technical experts.

 To help make standards projects more focused and timely, Federal agencies participating in the work of SDOs should make clear and comprehensive contributions with regard to the scope of cybersecurity standardization projects, as well as target dates to complete those projects.
 Federal agencies should make timely technical contributions to draft standards for cybersecurity to ensure that the resulting standards are technically sound.

 Federal agencies should support and coordinate on the timely development of conformity and interoperability assessment schemes for cybersecurity (including international schemes), whether by private or public sector bodies, to accelerate the development and use of technically sound standards and standards-based products, processes and services (e.g., the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP)25, and where appropriate show preference in procurement for those suppliers that demonstrate conformance to such standards.

 Federal agencies should regularly promote close collaboration with the private sector in standards development for cybersecurity. This means that agencies should seek to build consensus rather than impose a preferred solution.

 Leveraging U.S. public and private sector collaboration in standards development for cybersecurity requires making maximum use of existing processes and, where necessary, establishing additional processes for effective communication on substance, strategy, and tactics between the USG and U.S. private sector standardization participants.

 The USG should ensure dialogue and information exchange takes place between senior Federal cybersecurity officials and their counterparts in key partner countries on cybersecurity standards development activities.

 The USG should also facilitate periodic reviews of coordination efforts between Federal agency staff and their foreign government counterparts on cybersecurity standards activities, focusing on lessons learned, highlighting useful collaborative mechanisms, and suggesting opportunities for improvement.

 The USG should encourage and support expanded standards training for Federal agency staff. Such training should cover: the impacts and benefits of cybersecurity standardization; the potential costs of failing to participate in cybersecurity standards development, revise standards when needed, and use such standards in their programmatic activities; and understanding the processes of various SDOs and how to influence successfully the content of standards to meet U.S. objectives.

o Standards training would help to ensure that Federal agency participants in cybersecurity standardization are aware of policy and technical developments impacting cybersecurity standardization, and are current on other skills and competencies needed for successful participation in cybersecurity standardization.

o Educating senior leadership of agencies regarding the value of standards work and the need for long-term consistency of investment would encourage Federal agencies to provide: (i) continuous support for their technical experts’ participation and leadership activities in mission critical SDOs, including SDO-specific training and mentoring; and (ii) generalized standards training to enhance their participants’ effectiveness in international standards development. Many SDOs offer training on their processes and on standards in general, which Federal agencies may be able to use.
 The USG should encourage privacy research and development to support standards and best practices that contribute to the improved identification of privacy risk and mitigation methods.

 Federal agencies participating in the work of SDOs should make technical contributions to draft standards to ensure that the resulting cybersecurity standards minimize privacy risks using a privacy risk management framework, while enabling information-sharing relating to cybersecurity and allowing the USG to combat cyber-enabled threats.

 Federal agencies should use relevant international standards for cybersecurity, where effective and appropriate, in their mission and policymaking activities. This includes both cybersecurity standards and standards from other domains that are relevant to cybersecurity.
 In accordance with U.S. laws and policy26, Federal agencies should use relevant international standards in their procurement and regulatory activities whenever possible.

 Where international standards are either not relevant, effective, and appropriate or do not exist, agencies should seek to work with the private sector to develop them through an SDO to promote global acceptance and then use them for achieving mission and policy objectives.

 To the extent that agencies believe that it is necessary to use U.S.-specific approaches, they should develop such approaches through open and transparent processes (e.g., notice-and-comment rulemaking) and seek to promote their adoption into the international standards ecosystem, where appropriate, to promote their use globally.

This report, which was drafted by the National Security Council (NSC) Cyber Interagency Policy Committee’s International Cybersecurity Standardization Working Group for the Administration, sets out proposed United States Government (USG) strategic objectives for pursuing the development and use of international standards for cybersecurity, and makes recommendations to achieve those objectives. Implementation of these recommendations—which cover interagency coordination, collaboration with the U.S. private sector and international partners, agency participation in international standards development, standards training and education, use of international standards to achieve mission and policy objectives, and other topics–will enable the development and execution of a wide-ranging United States Government cybersecurity standardization strategy.

The Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014 was signed into law by President Obama on December 18, 2014. Section 502 of the Act requires the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to work with relevant federal agencies to ensure interagency coordination “in the development of international technical standards related to information system security,” and develop and transmit to Congress a plan for ensuring such coordination within one year of enactment. Further, the Act instructs NIST to ensure consultation with “appropriate private sector stakeholders.” This report will also serve as the basis of the required report to Congress.

The Supplemental Information document (NISTIR 8074 Volume 2) provides additional background on the overall importance of standards and conformity assessment for global commerce and the status of international cybersecurity standardization.

Given the increasingly global, complex, and interconnected nature of the world economy, characterized by rapid advances in technology and use of commercial off the shelf products to assure cybersecurity and resilience, the use of international cybersecurity standards for information technologies (IT)1 and industrial control systems (ICS)2 are necessary for the cybersecurity and resilience of all U.S. information and communications systems and supporting infrastructures.

Cybersecurity relies upon a diverse set of standards including standards whose scopes are specific to one or more attributes of cybersecurity and standards from other domains that are relevant to cybersecurity.

The U.S. standardization community is comprised largely of non-governmental Standards Developing Organizations (SDOs). These groups are primarily shaped by industry (both U.S. and foreign), academic institutions, professional societies, consumer groups, and nonprofits and are motivated by market forces, public interest, and consumer protection. USG participation is motivated by the need to achieve economic, timely and effective solutions for mission and policy objectives. These diverse motivations are mutually beneficial.

The U.S. Government strategy is to leverage these motivations in the development and use of international standards to promote cybersecurity and resilience. Consistent with the goals of the USG to promote secure cyberspace, there are four fundamental interrelated USG strategic objectives in actively participating in the development and use of timely international standards for cybersecurity:

For purposes of this report, a standard is a document, established by consensus and approved by a recognized body, which provides for common and repeated use, rules, guidelines or characteristics for activities or their results, aimed at the achievement of the optimum degree of order in a given context.6 A standards developer is any organization that develops and approves standards using various methods to establish consensus among its participants. The use of such documentary consensus standards is voluntary.

Pursuant to U.S. laws and policy,7 federal agencies are required to use voluntary consensus standards in their procurement and regulatory activities, giving preference to international standards, except where inconsistent with law or otherwise impractical. Many SDOs operate through a process that is characterized by all or some of the following attributes: openness, balance, due process, ability to appeal, and consensus. Openness means that the procedures or processes used are open to interested parties. Such parties are provided meaningful opportunities to participate in standards development on a non-discriminatory basis. The procedures or processes for participating in standards development and for developing the standard are transparent. The standards development process should also be balanced. Specifically, there should be meaningful involvement from a broad range of parties, with no single interest dominating the decision-making. Due process should include documented and publicly available policies and procedures, adequate notice of meetings and standards development, sufficient time to review drafts and prepare views and objections, access to views and objections of other participants and a fair and impartial process for resolving conflicting views. An appeals process should be available for the impartial handling of procedural appeals. Consensus is defined as general agreement, but not necessarily unanimity. During the development of consensus, comments and objections are considered using fair, impartial, open, and transparent processes. These process attributes contribute to the technical soundness and market relevance of the published standards of an SDO.

The U.S. standards system differs significantly from the government-driven, centrally-coordinated standards systems common in many other countries. Within the United States, there are hundreds of SDOs, which are overwhelmingly private sector organizations, providing the infrastructure for the preparation of standards documents. USG personnel participate in SDO activities along with representatives from industry, academia, and other organizations and consumers. In many other countries' standards systems, the government plays a larger role in standards development-related activities, which provides those governments the ability to use standards to support domestic industrial and innovation policy, rather than to advance technical solutions in support of public policy goals. While Federal agencies possess certain responsibilities related to standards, such as in their own use of standards or in their development of technical regulations, there is a much greater reliance in the U.S. on the private sector, including companies and industry groups, academic institutions, professional societies, consumer groups, and other interested parties, in standards development. The United States Standards Strategy8, elaborated through a private and public sector partnership in 2000, and revised most recently in 2010, outlines the contribution of private-sector led standards development to overall competition and innovation in the U.S. economy and the imperative of public and private sector participation that is a central tenet of the U.S. approach to standardization.

Conformity assessment is activity that provides demonstration that specified requirements relating to a product, process, system, person or body are fulfilled. Conformity assessment activities can be performed by many types of organizations or individuals. Conformity assessment can be conducted by: (1) a first party, which is generally the supplier or manufacturer; (2) a second party, which is generally the purchaser or user of the product; (3) a third party, which is an independent entity that is generally distinct from the first or second party and has no interest in transactions between the two parties; and (4) the government, which has a unique role in conformity assessment activities related to regulatory requirements.

For example, conformance testing captures the technical description of the requirements in a standard and measures whether an implementation (product, process or service) faithfully fulfills these requirements. Conformance testing alone does not completely ensure the interoperability or performance of conforming products, processes, or services. Therefore, interoperability and performance testing are also important aspects for procurements. Interoperability testing tests one implementation with another to establish that they can work together properly. Performance testing measures the performance characteristics of an implementation, such as its throughput9 or response time,10 under various conditions.

In some instances, testing and attestation of products, processes, and services against established cybersecurity standards may help provide a level of assurance that a product, process, or service’s stated security claim is valid. An example is the USG requirement for using cloud products that meet Federal cloud security requirements. Commercial assessment organizations, which are accredited for assessing cloud security, determine if a cloud product conforms to the requirements. This can be more cost-effective for Federal agencies than developing in-house USG testing expertise.

Consistent with OMB Circular A-119, agencies retain the flexibility of choosing the appropriate conformity assessment programs—whether private, public, or some combination thereof—and tools to best achieve their objectives.

This section sets out core areas of cybersecurity that broadly influence the overall cybersecurity of products, processes, services, and organizations. USG technical experts have been participating in many core areas of cybersecurity standardization for decades. The resulting standards are largely being developed for the global marketplace generally and not just for federal networks and applications.16 Such standards provide the requirements for cybersecurity standards-based products, processes or services. As a consequence of participating in this standards work, the USG has acquired and accumulated competency in core areas of cybersecurity standardization, but the depth and breadth of this USG competency can rise and fall with time.

Core areas of cybersecurity standardization include: cryptographic techniques; cyber incident management; identity and access management; IT system security evaluation; information security management systems; network security; security automation and continuous monitoring; supply chain risk management; software assurance; and system security engineering. These areas, which are relevant for numerous applications, are discussed in detail in the Supplemental Information document (NISTIR 8074 Volume 2). Based upon legislative and policy mandates, there are a growing number of national priority applications for which the USG participates in the development of standards relevant to cybersecurity, including: cloud computing; emergency management; industrial control systems; health IT; smart grid; and voting. Such applications utilize cybersecurity standards in each of the listed core areas.

Worldwide, there are over 200 SDOs developing IT and ICS standards. Among those, there are dozens of SDOs developing cybersecurity standards, yet fewer SDOs may develop international cybersecurity standards. Some of the key SDOs directly involved in cybersecurity that may develop international standards are: the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP); the 3rd Generation Partnership Project 2 (3GPP2); the Alliance for Telecommunications Industry Solutions (ATIS); the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA); the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI); the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC); the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE); the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); the International Society of Automation (ISA); the International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission Joint Technical Committee 1 (ISO/IEC JTC 1), Information Technology; the International Organization for Standardization Technical Committee 68 (ISO TC 68), Financial Services; the International Telecommunication Union Radiocommunication Sector (ITU-R); the Object Management Group (OMG); the OpenID Foundation (OIDF); the Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards (OASIS); the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council (PCI SSC); SAE International; The Open Group; the Trusted Computing Group (TCG); the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C); and the WiMAX Forum. Collectively, these SDOs have many hundreds of cybersecurity standards projects under maintenance or development. Being able to influence cybersecurity standards development requires developing and maintaining effective liaisons and active engagements within and among these SDOs.

This status information in Table 1 represents a high-level standards gap analysis. “Standards Mostly Available” indicates that SDO-approved cybersecurity standards are for the most part available and standards-based implementations are available. However, the availability of standards means that such standards require continuous maintenance and updating/replacing based upon feedback from testing and deployments of standards-based products, processes, and services, as well as improvements in technology and the exploitation of those improvements by those engaging in cybercrime and cyberespionage. “Some Standards Available” indicates that some standards exist and have standards-based implementations, but there may be a need for additional standards and/or revisions to existing standards in this area. “Standards Being Developed” indicates that needed SDO-approved cybersecurity standards are still under development and that needed standards-based implementations are not yet available. “New Standards Needed” indicates that new cybersecurity standards development projects are starting to be considered by various SDOs.

Four observations can be made on the overall status of ongoing cybersecurity standardization. First, robust standardization activities in the listed core areas of cybersecurity standardization are undoubtedly necessary for ensuring interoperability, security, usability, and resilience. Second, as illustrated by the listed applications in Table 1, there is a mix of ongoing standardization and maintenance of existing standards that is necessary to sustain deployments of standards-based products, processes and services. Third, the standards produced by SDOs represent a point in time. They often need to evolve in a way that meets the challenges of the ever-changing threat landscape. Finally, while Table 1 is structured by applications, there are some cybersecurity standards that apply across the applications to the development and manufacturing of IT products (hardware and software), products that most if not all of these applications depend on.

The ten listed core areas of cybersecurity standardization are important areas but are not all inclusive. An augmented taxonomy for core areas of cybersecurity standardization could be an area for further work. The six examples of key applications that depend upon cybersecurity are also not all inclusive. Many other applications could be added, such as automotive, financial services, mobile, and Internet of Things (IoT). However, the listed ten core areas and six examples of key applications are considered sufficient for the purposes of capturing a snapshot of the status of cybersecurity standardization.

There are at least three active USG groups that provide for interagency coordination on standards-related matters. The Interagency Committee on Standards Policy (ICSP) provides advice and recommendations to the Secretary of Commerce and other Executive Branch agencies on matters related to standards policy that could impact Federal agencies’ participation in, and use of, standards. The Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) Subcommittee of the Trade Policy Staff Committee (TPSC), which is led by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), coordinates the development and implementation of USG positions relating to technical regulations, standards and conformity assessment procedures around the world. The JESC (Joint Enterprise Standards Committee) serves as the Department of Defense (DoD) information technology standards and Intelligence Community (IC) enterprise standards governance body. This forum collaborates and recommends common enterprise standards, profiles, and specifications for the respective DoD and IC information environments. Interagency coordination on standards-related matters also occurs in some subcommittees and working groups within the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC). Given the critical importance of cybersecurity standardization and its cross-cutting nature —which involves security, standards, innovation, competition, trade, privacy, law enforcement and national security, and other policy considerations –a higher-level interagency coordination mechanism is needed. Coordination by senior Federal cybersecurity officials under the auspices of the Executive Office of the President (EOP) would provide the necessary focus and resources to develop and implement a strategy for cybersecurity-related standardization, as well as ensure that the USG can respond to specific priority issues as they arise.

In addition to coordination among federal agencies, the USG needs to engage effectively with U.S. industry. There are several methods agencies use to engage and coordinate with external stakeholders. Agencies may choose to establish external advisory committees per the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), seek input using Federal Register Notice solicitations, use specific statutory or regulatory authority to create a forum — such as a private sector coordinating council — for obtaining input, establish a public-private partnership, or use some other method that provides all potential stakeholders an equal opportunity to provide input and share their perspectives. As an example of FACA committees, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) created Health IT Policy and Standards committees that make recommendations to the National Coordinator on policy and standards topics, including cybersecurity. In addition, in developing the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity under Executive Order 13636, NIST provided stakeholders with an equal opportunity to share their views and make contributions through a series of workshops and public comment periods on drafts.

For SDOs that use a national body member process, such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), there is already built-in U.S. coordination through U.S. mirror groups (e.g., U.S. Technical Advisory Groups (TAGs) for ISO technical committees and subcommittees). The State Department administers a FACA-based process for developing U.S. positions relating to standardization in the International Telecommunication Union’s Telecommunication Standardization Sector (ITU-T), a treaty-based United Nations organization. For SDOs that are based on an individual membership model, public-private sector coordination prior to technical committee meetings is not built-in, so this may be a particular area that could benefit from enhanced focus by the USG.
